261: A and C are correct. Amazon CloudFront can cache multiple versions of the content based on values such as the CloudFront-Is-Mobile-Viewer or User-Agent headers, so each device type gets its own cached object at the edge, which is what option A provides. A Lambda@Edge function, as in option C, runs at CloudFront edge locations and can inspect the User-Agent header of each viewer request to select and return the specific object variant appropriate for that device, giving fine-grained control without changing the origin infrastructure. Together these serve device-specific content to a global audience with low latency, whereas host-based or path-based routing on an NLB or Global Accelerator cannot distinguish device types.
262: A is correct because a VPC peering connection privately links two VPCs in the same Region using private IP addresses with no additional infrastructure to run, making it the most cost-effective way to connect a single App VPC to a single Cache VPC. Adding route table entries in both VPCs allows the application's EC2 instances to reach the ElastiCache cluster, and allowing inbound traffic on the ElastiCache cluster's security group from the application's security group provides the necessary access control. A Transit VPC adds cost and management overhead that is unnecessary for only two VPCs, and a peering connection itself has no security group to configure.
263: A and D are correct. Deploying an Amazon ECS cluster, as in option A, provides AWS's native container orchestration for the microservices. Deploying the ECS service with the Fargate launch type, as in option D, means AWS manages the underlying compute for each task, so the company does not have to provision, patch, or scale any infrastructure, while the desired task count of at least 2 provides availability and the service scales automatically. Options based on self-managed Kubernetes or the EC2 launch type require managing additional infrastructure, which the requirements prohibit.
264: D is correct because an Application Load Balancer continuously health checks the EC2 instances and automatically routes traffic only to healthy targets, eliminating the timeout errors caused by DNS resolving to unhealthy instances. Route 53 then points a single alias record at the ALB, which balances requests across healthy instances. Per-instance Route 53 records with health checks can remove unhealthy endpoints but do not provide load balancing or rapid traffic steering, and CloudFront is a caching service rather than an origin health manager.
265: C is correct because Amazon CloudFront delivers HTTPS content through its global edge locations, so content is served as close to users as possible with the least delivery time, and using the public ALB as the CloudFront origin provides a single secure entry point. Placing the EC2 instances in private subnets means they are not directly exposed to the internet, which makes this the most secure design, while the ALB in public subnets accepts and forwards traffic to them. Pointing CloudFront directly at EC2 instances bypasses the ALB's centralized security and health checking.
266: A is correct because AWS Global Accelerator uses static anycast IP addresses advertised from AWS edge locations and routes user traffic over the AWS global network to the closest healthy Regional endpoint, minimizing latency for a latency-sensitive gaming application. Adding a listener for the application port and attaching the ALB in each Region as an endpoint lets Global Accelerator continuously monitor endpoint health with routing controls and automatically direct traffic to healthy endpoints, exactly meeting the monitoring and redirection requirement. CloudFront is designed for caching HTTP content rather than optimizing arbitrary game traffic, and the other options do not provide health-based traffic steering.
267: D is correct because Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose is a fully managed delivery stream that captures the data in near real time, supports encryption, and delivers it to a centralized Amazon S3 location with automatic data format conversion to Apache Parquet. Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics then analyzes the streaming data in near real time as a fully managed service, so the solution has the least operational overhead. The options using an Amazon EMR cluster require provisioning and managing cluster infrastructure, and adding Lambda functions to invoke analysis adds unnecessary components.
268: A is correct because placing Amazon ElastiCache in front of the RDS for MySQL database caches frequently read data in memory, dramatically improving read response times for a read-heavy workload while requiring minimal change to the existing architecture. The application simply checks the cache before querying the database, which reduces database load and eliminates the delays and interruptions users are experiencing. RDS Proxy addresses connection pooling rather than read performance, and migrating to Lambda or DynamoDB would require major architectural changes.
269: C is correct because creating a read replica of the primary RDS database gives the business analysts a separate synchronized copy of the data on which to run their read-only SQL queries, offloading that workload from the production database and resolving the performance degradation. A read replica requires minimal change since the analysts simply point their queries at the replica endpoint while the web application continues using the primary unchanged. The other options require copying or transforming the data into a different technology, which involves far more change.
270: A is correct because client-side encryption encrypts the data locally before it is uploaded, guaranteeing the data is encrypted at rest before it ever reaches the S3 buckets, and combined with HTTPS for the transfer it also ensures encryption in transit. Server-side encryption options, including SSE-S3 and KMS keys, only encrypt the data after it arrives at S3, which does not meet the requirement that the data be encrypted before upload.
271: C is correct because scheduled scaling lets the Auto Scaling group scale out to the exact required capacity at a set time, such as shortly before 1 AM when the nightly batch jobs begin, so full capacity is immediately available rather than being ramped up gradually over an hour. A scheduled scale-in action can then reduce capacity after the batch completes, keeping costs low the rest of the day. This is the most cost-effective approach for a workload with a predictable recurring start time and known peak, unlike raising minimum capacity, which would run instances around the clock.
272: B is correct because Amazon CloudFront caches the website's content at edge locations worldwide, so users far from us-west-1 are served from a nearby edge location instead of directly from the origin Region, without recreating the architecture in multiple Regions. Using the existing ALB as the origin preserves the current application setup, and configuring cache behavior to cache based on the Accept-Language request header lets CloudFront store and serve separate cached versions of the content for each language, efficiently supporting the multilingual requirement.
273: B is correct because an Amazon Aurora global database uses dedicated storage-based replication to a secondary Region with typical replication lag of under a second, keeping the DR Region's database up to date with the least possible latency. A warm standby deployment keeps a scaled-down but fully running copy of the infrastructure in the DR Region that can quickly scale up and take over, which delivers the lowest recovery time objective, matching the requirement for reduced capacity that can scale. Pilot light deployments require provisioning resources at failover time and yield a higher RTO, and RDS Multi-AZ only provides protection within a single Region.
274: B is correct because creating AMIs of the EC2 instances and copying them to a secondary Region preserves ready-to-launch machine images while consuming almost no running resources during normal operations, satisfying the requirement to use the fewest possible AWS resources. Automating the secondary Region deployment with AWS CloudFormation provides a managed, repeatable Infrastructure as Code approach that can provision the full environment quickly, enabling an RTO of less than 4 hours in an operationally efficient way. Custom Lambda scripts are harder to maintain and less reliable than CloudFormation, and keeping instances running in another Region or Availability Zone consumes continuous resources.
275: C is correct because a target tracking scaling policy automatically adjusts capacity to keep a chosen metric at a target value, and lowering the CPU threshold makes the Auto Scaling group add instances earlier as morning traffic ramps up, so capacity is in place before staff experience slowness. Decreasing the cooldown period allows successive scaling actions to happen more quickly during the rapid morning ramp, further accelerating scale-out, while the target tracking policy still scales the group down to 2 instances overnight to keep costs to a minimum.
276: A and D are correct. Configuring storage Auto Scaling on the RDS for Oracle instance, as in option A, makes the database automatically increase its allocated storage as it approaches the limit, resolving the storage exhaustion without manual intervention. Configuring the Auto Scaling group to use average CPU as its scaling metric, as in option D, gives the group a workload-driven metric that automatically adds EC2 instances as traffic steadily increases. Aurora cannot be used because it does not support Oracle PL/SQL functions, and a low-storage alarm only notifies rather than resolving the issue, while average free memory is not a reliable EC2 scaling metric.
277: D is correct because Amazon S3 provides durable, highly scalable object storage at a much lower cost than EFS Standard for large video files that are uploaded once and then processed. During processing, files can be temporarily moved onto an EBS volume attached to the processing server, providing fast local block storage for the transcoding work, and the EBS volume only needs to be paid for while in use. This avoids the continuously expensive EFS Standard capacity costs while still supporting the processing workflow.
278: B and E are correct. Amazon DynamoDB, as in option B, delivers single-digit millisecond latency for high-traffic queries, can model hierarchical relationships using partition and sort keys, and supports encryption at rest to protect sensitive employee data, while a monthly export to Amazon S3 preserves the data for further processing. Amazon Macie, as in option E, uses machine learning to discover sensitive data such as financial information, and integrating Macie findings with Amazon EventBridge enables a rule to send monthly notifications through an Amazon SNS subscription, which delivers the required email messages.
279: A is correct because AWS Backup provides a centralized, fully managed way to schedule backups of the DynamoDB table on the first day of each month through a backup plan. The plan's lifecycle policy can transition backups to cold storage after 6 months to reduce cost while keeping them available, and setting the retention period to 7 years automatically retains each backup for the required duration. The other options require building and maintaining custom scripts or CLI commands, which is error-prone, and DynamoDB on-demand backups do not natively support the required transition and retention rules.
280: B is correct because Amazon Athena is a serverless interactive query service that runs standard SQL directly against data stored in Amazon S3, making it ideal for analyzing the CloudFront logs already in the bucket with no infrastructure to manage. Amazon QuickSight is AWS's managed business intelligence service that visualizes the Athena query results and builds the required dashboards for advanced analysis. AWS Glue is an ETL and catalog service rather than a visualization tool, and DynamoDB is a NoSQL database that cannot run standard SQL against S3 logs.
